claims.text: Replacing or modifying some original ligands with stronger electron-donating groups increases electron donation to the transition-metal center.
Greater ligand electron donation increases electron density at the metal center.
Increased electron density at the metal center stabilizes key reactive intermediate oxidation states.
Stabilization of reactive intermediates mitigates catalyst deactivation through overoxidation.
Stronger electron-donating ligands improve oxidation-product selectivity.
Stronger electron-donating ligands improve catalyst durability.
Modified catalysts will produce a larger fraction of the desired oxidation product than catalysts with the original ligand environment.
Modified catalysts will degrade more slowly than catalysts with the original ligand environment.
Spectroscopic measurements such as XPS or UV-vis can be used to infer changes in metal-center electron density or d-orbital occupancy.
The proposed effect is expected under moderate-temperature and moderate-pressure oxidation conditions in which electron-transfer steps are rate limiting.
The hypothesis is expected to apply when oxidation performance is dominated by electronic-structure effects.
High temperatures, strong support interactions, or alternative reaction mechanisms may prevent the proposed ligand-electronic effect from governing performance.
